architecture.mechanism: Impact loading combined with high surface traction and contact pressure initiates micro-cracks and white etching areas (WEAs) at non-metallic inclusions, which propagate as white etching crack (WEC) networks and cause subsurface-driven surface flaking under rolling contact fatigue.
architecture.intervention: Modify the bearing raceway surface finish to lower surface traction (e.g., controlled micro-dimpling, superfinishing, or a low-friction DLC/tungsten-disulfide-based tribological coating) and add a sacrificial/viscosity-index-improver additive package to the gear oil that cushions transient impact spikes in the lubrication path (e.g., high-VI PAO with transient impact-absorbing VI improver and reduced traction coefficient), so that the combination of impact energy, contact pressure, and sliding traction at subsurface inclusions is suppressed.
architecture.expected_effect: Suppression of inclusion-initiated micro-cracks and WEA/WEC network formation under variable (impact-containing) load cycles, thereby delaying subsurface-driven surface flaking and extending bearing service life.
architecture.falsification_test: Run twin-disc RCF tests on standard and surface-modified/lubricant-modified bearing-steel specimens at matched Hertzian contact pressure, using a superimposed cyclic radial impact load representative of wind-turbine variable loading. After a fixed number of load cycles (e.g., 1e7), section and metallographically quantify the number density of inclusion-initiated micro-cracks and WEAs/WECs; the intervention is supported only if the modified specimens show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., ≥50% lower crack/WEA density) relative to the baseline, with no increase in surface-initiated fatigue.
